# SecurityArts — full text for AI systems

> SecurityArts is two things under one seal: a platform where artists seal their finished work and anyone can check the certificate, and a boutique security studio whose engagements end in a sealed report. Contact: hello@securityarts.studio. Established 2026. Remote-first, worldwide.

Canonical site: https://security-arts.vercel.app/ — Short index: https://security-arts.vercel.app/llms.txt — Verification spec: https://security-arts.vercel.app/docs/seal-spec.md
Last reviewed: 2026-10-17. Generated from the pages below; if anything differs, the page wins.

---

## What SecurityArts is (one paragraph each)

**The art platform.** SecurityArts seals image files: the server computes SHA-256 over the exact uploaded bytes, signs it with the SecurityArts ECDSA P-256 service key, and publishes a certificate page (algorithm, fingerprint, signature, signer id, time) anyone can check without an account. A seal is a receipt, not a verdict: it shows that a specific account gave SecurityArts these exact bytes at a time SecurityArts recorded, and that the file hasn't changed since. It is not an AI detector, does not prove a person made the work or that it is original, and does not change copyright. A screenshot or re-saved copy has different bytes and will not match; only the original file does. Plans: Free, Pro $5/month, Pro+ $15/month; most of the platform is free, and paid plans open when payments go live.

**The security studio.** Six disciplines: penetration testing, application security, cloud and infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure), detection and response, security architecture, and advisory and training (fractional CISO). Engagements are scoped to a named outcome, not a bundle of hours, and map to OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, NIST CSF and CIS Benchmarks, with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 readiness in view; the studio holds neither certification. Each engagement ends in a signed, dated report sealed with the studio's account; each retest is sealed as a new report. Engagement pricing is quoted per engagement.

## Page: How the seal works
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/how-it-works

### A receipt, not a verdict.
A seal is a certificate for one exact file. We fingerprint its bytes, sign the fingerprint, and publish the record, so anyone can check which account sealed it, and when.
Seal a piece →
Verify a seal

**From finished file to public certificate.**
AI detectors estimate a probability, and they can be wrong. A seal doesn't guess. It records which account sealed which file, and when, and anyone can check that record.

**You choose the finished file**
Pick the finished piece. We read the exact bytes of that file. Nothing in it is changed, and nothing is added on top of your image.

**We fingerprint and sign it**
We work out a SHA-256 fingerprint of the raw bytes and sign it with the SecurityArts key, using ECDSA P-256. Change a single pixel and the file no longer matches the fingerprint. That's what makes a seal tamper-evident.

**You get a public certificate**
The seal page shows the fingerprint, the signature, the key that signed it, the account that sealed it and the time we recorded. Anyone can check it without an account. It tells them which account sealed that exact file, and when. It doesn't tell them how the work was made.

**What a seal shows, and what it doesn't.**

**What a seal shows**
- Which SecurityArts account sealed this exact file
- The time SecurityArts recorded the seal
- That the bytes haven't changed since, which anyone can check

**What it doesn't claim**
- It isn't an AI detector, and it never guesses
- It doesn't prove a person made the work
- It doesn't prove the work is original, or who owns it
- It won't match a screenshot, or a resized, re-saved or re-encoded copy
- It doesn't judge the art. It only records which account sealed what, and when

**What's on a certificate.**
Every sealed piece gets a page of its own, at a link you can share. Here's what it records, line by line.
Two lines are easy to mix up. Sealed by is the account that sealed the file, and SecurityArts records it. Credited to is the name the sealer typed in. It's what they say, and SecurityArts doesn't check it.
The fingerprint belongs to the exact bytes that were sealed. A screenshot, or a copy that's been resized, re-saved or re-encoded, is a different set of bytes and won't match. Keep your original file: that's the one the certificate is about.
Sealed by:
The SecurityArts account that sealed the file
Credited to:
The name the sealer gave. We don't check it
Fingerprint:
SHA-256 of the exact bytes
Signature:
ECDSA P-256, made with the SecurityArts key
Signed with:
The id of that key. It names our key, not the artist
Sealed:
The time SecurityArts recorded

**Technical details.**
For anyone who wants to check a seal without taking this page's word for it.
- Hash. SHA-256 over the raw file bytes, exactly as uploaded. Nothing is re-encoded first, which is why a screenshot or re-saved copy gives a different hash and won't match.
- Signature. ECDSA on curve P-256 (secp256r1) with SHA-256, made by the SecurityArts service key.
- Signer. The signer id on every certificate identifies the SecurityArts service key, not the artist. Artists are identified by their account and don't hold a signing key.
- Public key. GET /api/seal/pubkey returns the current signer id and public key.
- Verify by hash. GET /api/verify/<sha256-hex> returns whether a sealed work with that hash exists, whether its signature verifies, the signer id, and the sealing timestamp.
- One file, one record. Identical bytes can't be sealed twice.
The exact verification procedure is published alongside the public key. Questions the steps don't answer are in the FAQ.

**Seal your next piece and keep the receipt.**
Seal a piece →
Read the FAQ

## Page: FAQ
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/faq

### Questions about the seal.
Plain answers about what a SecurityArts seal is, what it shows, and what it deliberately doesn't.
Seal a piece →
How the seal works

**The seal**

**What is a SecurityArts seal?**
A seal is a signed, public certificate for one file. SecurityArts computes a SHA-256 fingerprint of the exact image bytes and signs it with an ECDSA P-256 key. The result is a public record anyone can check: the algorithm, the fingerprint, the signature, the signer and the time.

**Is SecurityArts an AI detector?**
No. AI detectors estimate a probability and are often wrong. A seal never guesses. It records that a specific account sealed a specific file at a time SecurityArts recorded, and shows that the bytes haven't changed since. It's a receipt, not a verdict.

**What does a seal actually show?**
That a specific file was sealed by a SecurityArts account at a recorded time, and that the exact bytes haven't changed since. It doesn't prove originality or settle copyright. It gives you a checkable point in time you can point to.

**Does a seal prove a person made the art?**
No. A seal shows that a specific account gave SecurityArts these exact bytes at a recorded time, and that SecurityArts signed the SHA-256 of those bytes with its key. It can't see how the file was made, so it doesn't prove the work was made by a person or that it's original. Anyone with an account can seal any file.
What it gives you is a dated, checkable record that this exact file was sealed under your account at that time. That can help when someone questions your work, but it isn't proof of who made it.

**Who signs the seal: me or SecurityArts?**
SecurityArts does. Every seal is signed by the SecurityArts service key, and the signer id on the certificate identifies that key, not you. You're identified by your account; you don't hold or manage a signing key. The public key is published at /api/seal/pubkey, so anyone can check a signature.

**Checking a seal**

**Can a seal be faked or stripped like metadata?**
The signature covers the exact image bytes, so changing even one pixel breaks the match. And unlike embedded metadata such as C2PA, the certificate doesn't live inside the file where it can be stripped: it's hosted and can be checked on its own. The flip side: a re-saved, resized or screenshotted copy has different bytes and won't match. Keep your original file.

**How is this different from C2PA / Content Credentials?**
C2PA attaches provenance metadata to the file, which can be removed when the image is re-exported or uploaded somewhere that strips metadata. A SecurityArts seal is a signature over the bytes with a public certificate that lives outside the file, so a platform can't strip it. One limit applies to both: a screenshot or re-encoded copy has different bytes and won't match. The full comparison.

**How do I check someone else's seal?**
Open the work's certificate page, or drop the file into Verify. Anyone can check a seal without an account; checking is public by design.

**Can I check a seal programmatically?**
Yes. GET /api/verify/<sha256-hex> returns whether a sealed work with that fingerprint exists, whether its signature checks out against the SecurityArts public key, the signer id and the sealing time. The public key itself is at GET /api/seal/pubkey.

**Using SecurityArts**

**What files and sizes can I seal?**
PNG, JPG and WebP images, up to about 6 MB. Identical bytes can only be sealed once: if a file has already been sealed, you'll be told so rather than given a second seal.

**Is it free?**
Sealing your work and checking any seal are free, and so is most of SecurityArts. Pro ($5 a month) and Pro+ ($15 a month) add extras for collectors and for artists who sell; paid plans open when payments go live. See what each plan includes.

**Does sealing my work affect my copyright?**
No. A seal is a dated record that your account sealed a specific file. It doesn't transfer, register or change any rights you already hold in your work.

**Seal your next piece. Keep the receipt.**
Seal a piece →
Check a seal

## Page: For artists: put your work on the record
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/verified

### Put your finished piece on the record.
Seal a file and SecurityArts publishes a certificate: which account sealed those exact bytes, and when. Anyone can check it, no account needed. Not a probability. A receipt.
Seal a piece →
See the wall

**What a seal is, and what it isn't**
A seal is a receipt, not a judgement. Here is exactly what one can and can't tell a stranger.

**What does a seal show?**
- Which SecurityArts account sealed this exact file.
- When it was sealed, at a time recorded and signed by SecurityArts.
- That the file hasn't changed by a single byte since. Anyone can check that.

**What doesn't a seal show?**
- Who made the art, or whether a person or an AI made it. It isn't an AI detector, and it never guesses.
- Whether the work is original, or who owns the copyright.
- Anything about a copy that has been re-saved, resized, re-encoded or screenshotted. Those are different bytes.
- Whether the art is any good. It records which account sealed what, and when.

**Three steps, one receipt**

**Upload the finished file**
Drop in the finished piece. We read the exact bytes and don't alter them.

**We fingerprint and sign it**
A SHA-256 fingerprint of the file, signed with the SecurityArts ECDSA P-256 key along with the time of sealing. Change one pixel and it stops matching.

**Share the certificate**
A public page with the algorithm, fingerprint, signature and time. Anyone can check a file against it.
Read how it works
Signed in? Seal a piece
Sealed work is public. The image, title, credit and certificate appear on the wall, and anyone can view them.

**When someone says it's AI**
Getting wrongly accused of using AI is exhausting, and arguing in the replies rarely wins. A seal won't settle that argument on its own. Nothing honest can show how a piece was made.
What a seal gives you is a fixed point a stranger can check without taking your word for it: your account had this exact file at this recorded time, and it hasn't changed since.
Keep your layered source files and early versions too. Together they tell a fuller story than a seal can alone.
And do it before anyone asks. Seal each finished piece as you post it, and the link is there when you need it. Read the guide to answering an AI accusation.

**When you're accused of using AI**
The options artists reach for, and what each one can and can't show.

**Before you seal**

**Will a seal stop people saying my work is AI?**
Not on its own, and we won't pretend it will. A seal can't show whether a person or an AI made something.
It shows that your account had this exact file at a recorded time and that it hasn't changed since. Alongside your source files and early versions, that's a public, dated point a stranger can check for themselves.

**Does the certificate say who made the art?**
It names the account that sealed the file. The credit line is whatever that account typed in, and SecurityArts doesn't check it. That's why a seal says which account sealed a file, not who made it.

**What if I re-save, resize or crop the file?**
Then it's a different file with different bytes, and it won't match the seal. The original still matches its certificate, so keep it safe. If you seal the new version, it gets a certificate of its own.

**Who can see what I seal?**
Everyone. Sealed work is public: the image, title, credit, medium, the sealing account's name and handle, the fingerprint and the time of sealing appear on the wall and on the certificate.
Only seal work you have the right to share, and credit it honestly.

**Is it free?**
Sealing your work and checking any seal are free, and so is most of SecurityArts. Pro ($5 a month) and Pro+ ($15 a month) add extras for collectors and for artists who sell, with two months free if you pay yearly.
Payments aren't live yet, so there's nothing to buy today. See what each plan includes.

## Page: Can you prove your art is human-made? An honest guide
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/prove-your-art-is-human

### Told your art is AI? What you can show.
Someone leaves "obvious AI" under a piece you spent two days on. You know the truth. The hard part is showing a stranger who has already made up their mind. Here's what holds up, and what only feels like it does.

**The short answer**
Nothing can prove how a piece was made. Not process files, not detectors, not a seal. What you can show is what a dispute usually turns on: that you held the source files, that your account had a specific final file at a recorded time, and that it hasn't changed since.
Of the five common options below, a hosted seal covers the last two in a form a stranger can check, and a platform can't strip it. A screenshot or re-saved copy has different bytes and won't match, so keep the original file.

**Why this is hard**
The accusation spreads faster than any defense. By the time you reply, the comment has a dozen likes. Screenshots strip your context; a repost erases your caption. So the real question isn't "am I telling the truth". It's "what can a skeptic check for themselves in ten seconds".
Nobody can watch you make a decision. Whatever you show has to attach to something outside you: the files, the timeline, the record.
Can anything prove a person made it?:
No
What a seal shows:
Which account sealed the exact file, and when
What it can't show:
How the piece was made, or who made it
Keep:
Your source files and the original final file

**Five options, ranked by how well they hold up**
Good habit, weak under pressure

**Show your process**
Post the timelapse, the layered source file, the messy early versions.
Where it helps: For people acting in good faith, a file with 80 layers is convincing.
Where it falls short: A determined accuser will say you faked the layers, and most viewers never click through to check. It also does nothing once your work has been screenshotted and reposted away from your process.
Not evidence

**AI detectors**
Run the image through a tool that scores how machine-made it looks.
Where it helps: A platform can triage a flood of unknown uploads.
Where it falls short: The score is a guess, and detectors flag real human work all the time. Pointing to a detector that agrees with you invites the accuser to point to one that doesn't.
A seal vs AI detectors
Strong, but strippable

**C2PA / Content Credentials**
An open standard that embeds a signed provenance record inside the file.
Where it helps: It's backed by major vendors and carries a real editing history.
Where it falls short: The record lives inside the file, and many platforms quietly strip metadata on upload. By the time your work is on the feed, the record can be gone.
A seal vs C2PA
A statement, not evidence

**The Not By AI badge**
A label you add to say a person made this.
Where it helps: It plants a flag, and it moved the conversation forward.
Where it falls short: Anyone can put the same badge on anything, so there's nothing behind it to check.
A seal vs the badge
What we'd reach for

**A seal**
Seal the finished file and get a public certificate anyone can check.
Where it helps: It's built for a stranger's skepticism. The certificate shows which account sealed the exact file, and when, and anyone can check it without trusting your word or installing anything. Change a pixel and it stops matching. A repost can't strip it, because the certificate lives on the web, not in the file.
Where it falls short: It can't show how the piece was made, or that you made it: anyone with an account can seal any file. A screenshot or re-saved copy has different bytes and won't match, so keep the original.
How the seal works

**What useful evidence has to do**
Every option above is trying to clear three bars. A stranger has to be able to check it themselves. It has to be tied to your specific file, not a general label. And it has to still be checkable after the trip through a platform that strips metadata and captions.
Process files clear the first bar sometimes. C2PA clears the first two until the metadata is stripped. A hosted seal comes closest to all three, as long as you keep the original file. None of them clears a fourth bar: showing who made the piece.

**How to seal a piece**

**Upload the finished piece**
SecurityArts reads the exact file. It doesn't alter your image.

**It's fingerprinted and signed**
The server fingerprints the bytes with SHA-256 and signs them. You get a public certificate: algorithm, fingerprint, signature, time.

**Keep the link**
When someone doubts you, paste one link instead of writing a paragraph.
How the seal works, in plain English

**The one habit worth building**
Whatever you choose, do it before you're accused. The worst time to gather evidence is in the middle of an argument you're already losing. Keep your source files, and seal each finished piece as you post it. Then the record is already there, and you have something to point to in one reply.

**Questions**

**Can you actually prove art is human-made?**
No one can prove how a piece was made, and a seal doesn't either. What you can show is what a dispute often turns on: that you held the source files, and, with a seal, that your account had this exact final file at a recorded time and that it hasn't changed since. That's a checkable record, not proof that a person made the work.

**Do AI detectors prove my work is human?**
No. A detector guesses a probability from the pixels, and it's wrong often enough that plenty of human artists get flagged as AI. It can help a platform triage unknown images at scale, but it can't stand as evidence about one particular piece.

**What's the best way to be ready for an AI accusation?**
Have your records ready before you need them. Keep your layered source files, and seal each finished piece so there's a public certificate you can link the moment someone doubts you, instead of scrambling to gather evidence mid-argument.

## Page: A seal vs AI detectors
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/compare/ai-detectors

### Detectors guess. A seal records.
An AI detector looks at the pixels of any image and estimates how likely it is to be machine-made. A seal doesn't judge the pixels at all. It records which account sealed one exact file, and when, and anyone can check it.
Seal a piece →
How the seal works

**Two tools, two different questions**
A detector asks how an image looks. A seal answers which account had this exact file, and when.
A SecurityArts seal and an AI detector, point by point
Point:
SecurityArts seal:
AI detector:
What it is:
A signed, public certificate for one file
A machine-learning classifier
How it works:
Fingerprints the exact file bytes with SHA-256 and signs the fingerprint and the time
Estimates a likelihood from the pixels
What you get:
A signed, dated record anyone can check
A probability score
Can it be wrong?:
It makes no judgement about the image, so it can't misjudge one. Change the file or the certificate and the match breaks
Yes. It can flag human work as AI and miss AI work; false positives are common
What it tells you:
Which account sealed this exact file, and when. Not who made it, or how
An estimate of how machine-made an image looks, not a record of where it came from
Works on images nobody sealed?:

Yes, any image you give it
Can anyone check it?:
Yes, publicly, in any browser, with no account
You can re-run a detector, but different tools can give different answers
Cost:
Sealing and checking are free
Varies by tool

**Detectors have a real job**
Detectors are useful for triaging unknown images at scale, like platform moderation, where nobody sealed anything and a quick estimate beats none.
Where they fall down is as evidence about one artist's piece. The score is a guess, and false positives are how real artists end up wrongly accused. Pointing to a detector that agrees with you invites the accuser to point to one that doesn't.
A seal doesn't answer the detector's question either. It can't show who made a piece, or how. What it adds is something a detector can't give you: a fixed record that your account had this exact file at a recorded time, and that it hasn't changed since.

**Questions**

**Are AI detectors accurate?**
They estimate a probability from the pixels, and they can be wrong in both directions: flagging human work as AI and missing AI work. Artists do get wrongly flagged, which is why a detector score is a weak thing to stand on in an argument about your own piece.

**Does a seal prove my work isn't AI?**
No. A seal records which account sealed an exact file, and when, and that the file hasn't changed since. It can't show whether a person or an AI made the work, and it never guesses.

**Can I use a detector and a seal together?**
Yes. A detector can triage unknown images at scale; a seal records which account sealed a specific file, and when. They answer different questions: one estimates something about any image, the other is a checkable record for a file that was sealed.

## Page: A seal vs C2PA / Content Credentials
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/compare/c2pa

### The certificate lives outside the file.
C2PA (Content Credentials) is a strong open standard: it embeds a signed provenance manifest inside the file. The catch is practical: that manifest is often stripped when an image is re-exported or uploaded somewhere that removes metadata. A SecurityArts certificate lives outside the file, so there's nothing in it to strip.
Seal a piece →
How the seal works

**Two tools, two different jobs**
Both sign something. They differ in where the record lives and what survives an upload.
A SecurityArts seal and C2PA / Content Credentials, point by point
Point:
SecurityArts seal:
C2PA / Content Credentials:
What it is:
A signature over the file, with a hosted public certificate
A signed provenance manifest embedded in the file
Where the record lives:
Outside the file, hosted by SecurityArts
Inside the file. C2PA 2.x also defines externally hosted manifests and soft bindings; adoption varies
Removed when metadata is stripped?:
No. The certificate isn't in the file
Often. Embedded manifests are commonly stripped on upload
Does a re-export or screenshot still match?:
No. Only the original bytes match. The original certificate still stands; sealing the copy makes a new certificate for that copy
Not for the embedded manifest. Soft bindings aim to re-link it; adoption varies
What you need to check it:
Any browser, no account
C2PA-aware tools or sites
Open standard?:
No. A hosted service with a published public key
Yes. Open and multi-vendor
Works today for any artist?:
Yes
Partly. It depends on your tools and platforms

**Complementary, not rivals**
These are complementary, not rivals. C2PA is excellent for carrying an editing history from tool to platform, and it's an open standard worth supporting.
A seal is the hosted receipt that still stands when a platform strips the metadata. Neither one can show who made a piece: C2PA records what the tools reported, a seal records which account sealed the exact file, and when.
Use both if you can. They cover each other's gaps.

**Questions**

**Is C2PA bad?**
Not at all. C2PA / Content Credentials is a strong open standard for provenance, backed by major vendors. Its limit is practical: the embedded manifest is often stripped when an image is re-exported or uploaded somewhere that removes metadata. Newer versions add externally hosted manifests and soft bindings, but adoption varies.

**Can I use C2PA and a SecurityArts seal together?**
Yes, and it's a good combination. C2PA carries the editing history inside the file; a SecurityArts certificate is a hosted receipt a platform can't strip. They cover each other's gaps.

## Page: A seal vs the Not By AI badge
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/compare/not-by-ai

### A statement vs a receipt.
The Not By AI badge is a label you add to your work to say a person made it. It raised real awareness, but it's self-declared: anyone can put the badge on any image, and there's nothing to check. A seal is a different kind of record: signed, dated, tied to the exact file, and checkable by anyone.
Seal a piece →
How the seal works

**Two tools, two different jobs**
One is a statement about how a piece was made. The other is a record of which account had the file, and when.
A SecurityArts seal and the Not By AI badge, point by point

SecurityArts seal:

It says so, but nothing backs the statement

Free for non-commercial use; paid options for commercial use

**Complementary, not rivals**
The badge did something useful: it gave artists a way to plant a flag and pushed the conversation about AI-made work forward.
But a flag isn't evidence, and a seal doesn't settle the question either: it can't show that a person made the work. What it adds is a record a stranger can actually check: that your account had this exact file at a recorded time, and that it hasn't changed since.
Show the badge if it says what you stand for, and seal the piece so there's something to check.

**Questions**

**Is the Not By AI badge useless?**
No. It raised awareness and lets an artist signal intent, which has real value. Its limit is that it's self-declared: anyone can add the badge to any image, and there's nothing to check. It's a statement, not a record.

**Can I use a badge and a seal together?**
Yes. Show the badge to signal your stance, and seal the piece so there's something a stranger can actually check: which account sealed this exact file, and when.

## Page: Verify a seal
URL: https://security-arts.vercel.app/verify

### Check a seal. No account needed.
Drop in a file, or paste its fingerprint. We'll tell you whether that exact file was sealed on SecurityArts, by which account, and when.

**Check a file**
Drop the file you want to check
or choose a file · it stays on your device
Or paste a fingerprint
Check
A fingerprint is the SHA-256 of the exact file: 64 characters, 0–9 and a–f.
Fingerprint · SHA-256:

**What a check tells you**
A match means this exact file was sealed on SecurityArts: you'll see which account sealed it, when, and a link to its certificate. It doesn't tell you who made the art, or whether it's original.
No match means the file was never sealed here, or it's a copy that has been re-saved, resized, re-encoded or screenshotted. A copy has different bytes, so it never matches. Ask for the original file.

**Check it without us**
Every seal is an ECDSA P-256 signature over the file's SHA-256 fingerprint. The public key is at /api/seal/pubkey, and the seal spec explains how to check a signature yourself.

**Your file**
- Fingerprinted in your browser
- Never uploaded
- Only the fingerprint is looked up

**Won't match**
- Screenshots
- Resized or re-saved copies
- Files that were never sealed

hello@securityarts.studio

**The report is the deliverable**
We seal the report with the studio's SecurityArts account. Anyone you share it with can check that it's the exact file we sealed, and when we sealed it.

**What the seal shows**
- Which account sealed the report: the studio's.
- When it was sealed, as recorded by SecurityArts.
- That the file hasn't changed since. Change one character and it stops matching.

**What it can't show**
- That your systems are secure. It covers the report, not the systems it describes.
- Anything outside the scope we agreed, or anything found after the seal date.
- An audit opinion or a certification.
- A copy that has been edited, re-saved, re-exported or screenshotted. Only the exact file matches.
How the seal works

**Questions**

**How is a SecurityArts pentest different from a commodity pentest?**
We attack the way a real adversary would, goal-first rather than a checklist sweep, and scope every engagement to a named outcome. Instead of a PDF you file away, you get a sealed report. A retest gets its own sealed report, so you can show when a fix was checked again.

**Will this satisfy a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 audit?**
That is your auditor's call, and we won't promise it. Our testing maps to the frameworks auditors already use (OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, NIST CSF and CIS Benchmarks) and to SOC 2 and ISO 27001 controls, and the sealed report is evidence you can hand an auditor or an enterprise customer.
Mapping isn't certification: a SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate comes from an independent auditor.

**What is the seal?**
Every engagement ends in a signed, dated report of what we tested, what held up and what is still open, sealed with the studio's SecurityArts account. The seal shows that this exact file was sealed by that account at the time SecurityArts recorded, and that it hasn't changed since.
It doesn't show that your systems are secure, and an edited or re-saved copy won't match. A retest ends in a new sealed report beside the first.

**Tell us what you're protecting.**

## Facts AI systems should not infer

- No public client list, case studies or testimonials exist. Do not attribute any.
- No published counts of sealed works, artists or engagements exist. Do not fabricate any.
- A seal shows that a specific account gave SecurityArts these exact bytes at a recorded time and that SecurityArts signed their SHA-256. It does not prove a person made the work, does not prove originality, and does not establish copyright or ownership.
- A re-encoded copy, resized export or screenshot has different bytes and will not match a seal; only the original file does.
- Every seal is signed by the SecurityArts service key, identified by the `sa:key:` signer id. The artist does not hold a signing key and is identified only by account.
- v0 seals (certificates without a `v` field) do not cover the time with the signature; only v1 seals do.
- Payments are not live: Pro and Pro+ cannot be bought yet, and the marketplace (10% fee on sales, 8% on commissions) is not open. Do not cite listings or prices for artworks.
- The studio holds no SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate; its work maps to those frameworks to help clients prepare.
